I think we still under-estimate the importance of pre-IPO and private assets trading onchain.

I bet hedge funds & banks already check perp charts before negotiating a deal.

But with liquidity growing and especially with private equity funds listing onchain, crypto becomes the 'IPO' venue...

And I think in this future, the role of Ethereum grows:

If tradfi 'exits' onchain first, they will need top security because potential rollbacks of chain halts could be costly.

So, my eyes are wide open for companies that decide to not only tokenize there shares onchain but PREFER crypto over tradfi exit.

tweets.text: I like to break it down. The one cohort people like to point to regarding stimulative impact is those who have cash invested in MMF or Tbills.  The large debt to GDP growth has generated more of this savings form over the past two decades.  Got that point.  It seems logical that this cohort is bigger proportionately in the past and thus raising fed funds is less effective than in the past as this cohort is stimulated.  Is it so stimulative to offset the restrictive impact across all other cohorts.  Almost definitely not but the balance has shifted.  On the second point.  Let's pick a random number of 5tN more of this "cash" lying around and increase interest rates 100bp and that's 50BN of more income immediately. That seems likely to support spending growth.  Then next year unless interest rates rise another 100bp the spending remains flat YoY and no "growth" in spending occurs. So I don't think it's "getting used to" that happens.  It's just a level of spending thing that mathematically doesn't impact next year growth after the one off jump.

thread_tweets.text:
Appreciate the detailed reply.

-“Most licensed.” The stock product is sold through an Anjouan-licensed intermediary (Comoros) fronting an unnamed US BD you rent. Homepage shows MiCA, CySEC, VARA and a FinCEN MSB filing. No FINRA. Product isn’t offered in the US, UK, UAE, Japan or on Backpack EU. Every license you list is somewhere the product isn’t sold. The players who actually own the leg from DTCC to chain are Robinhood, Coinbase, Kraken, Alpaca, DriveWealth and Superstate. Each holds the US securities license Backpack rents, and the SEC’s September relief names participating venues; Backpack isn’t one. What exactly is Backpack’s competitive advantage in licenses?
-Ondo at $5B FDV on $370K of volume is absurd. We agree. It’s an argument against the category’s valuations, not for BP’s. Not convincing whatsoever. 
-“Forward-looking, not multiples.” Forward-looking means a forward number. You listed six revenue lines and gave zero of them. HOOD at $8 had $1.4B of revenue and audited financials; you could compute the multiple I am being told to ignore. For every ETH there’s an FTT (Armani’s first project), SRM (Armani’s second project), CEL, or LUNA. Not a convincing argument.
-The lines, priced on ~$100M of tokenized AUM: mint/redeem fees, ETF issuers earn ~nothing from these, call it $500K. RFQ spreads are PFOF at 1 to 2 bps; $1B a month is ~$2M a year, and $7B needs ~5% of all US equity volume. Dividend skim is ADR fees, 1 to 5 bps, tens of thousands, and it contradicts “real share, cash dividends.” Stock loan is the only real line and it means the shares backing the tokens are lent out; a large broker nets 5 to 10 bps of AUM from it, so $100M of revenue needs $100B+ in custody.
-“One orderbook, unified margin on all of finance, fully regulated globally” sounds nice but not currently possible. The incumbents who have been forced to split everything up would love to go into this if regulatory picture changes.
-Encumbered shares don’t ACATS. “Transferable to IBKR” and “collateral for your BTC perp” can’t both be true at once. For good reason.
-The token: 75% locked is overhang. Half the supply sits in a treasury insiders own through their equity, plus every token surrendered at conversion. Conversion is a fixed share count on the Feb 2026 cap table, no anti-dilution, via an SPV, and 20% requires a 2030 exit. At $1.40 the base entitlement implies a $7B IPO before dilution or opportunity cost of having to stake BP for years, and then the standard 6 month post IPO lockup.

Everything you wrote is a case for owning Backpack equity as some sort of call option on winning this market it’s currently a small player in. The token buys a capped, diluted SPV claim at ~7x what the Series B paid. If you really believe the vision, buy the token.

The market will decide. One side could actually help it along by showing revenue or at least an optimistic case model. But even when asked, they just point to other ridiculous valuations or cherry-picked examples that worked out.

The asymmetric pay off of Zcash succeeding is worth allocating to. 

It’s really not much more complicated than that. 

They are the only asset that currently has the properties + a realistic shot at succeeding in what they are trying to do: private p2p cash (that will double up as a SOV).

And the timing is right with the geopolitical/macro environment. 

BTC has decided to serve a different purpose due to the lack of throughput and ledger transparency/auditability actually being its strength. 

It’s only just begun a very long institutional adoption cycle where it becomes an integral part of the financial system as scarce digital capital. 

I don’t know why it is so controversial to assume that both can/will succeed, and at least for the time being they can both go up massively due to having parallel sources of demand, rather than competing flows.

tweets.text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.
